stem.en: Two identical hockey pucks are hit with the same force. Puck A slides on smooth ice; Puck B slides on rough concrete. Which puck travels farther before stopping, and why — in terms of Newton's first law?

text.en: Puck A (on ice) — a smaller friction force means a smaller net force decelerating it, so its velocity changes more slowly and it coasts farther before reaching zero.

feedback.en: Correct — same starting push, but a smaller unbalanced force means the first law's 'velocity stays put unless a net force acts' takes much longer to finish its job.

text.en: Puck B (on concrete) — more friction gives more grip, which helps push the puck forward for longer.

feedback.en: This has friction's direction backwards for this situation. Friction here opposes the puck's motion (it acts to slow the puck, not to help it along) — more friction means a bigger decelerating force, not a bigger 'grip-forward' push.

text.en: Both travel the same distance — the first law says the puck keeps its velocity until a force stops it, and friction is present in both cases, so it doesn't matter how much.

feedback.en: Right that friction is present in both cases, but the law cares about how BIG the net force is, not just whether one exists. A bigger friction force decelerates the puck faster, which is exactly why the surface matters here.

explanation.en: Newton's first law explains why a puck slows at all (an unbalanced force is acting) but the SIZE of that force decides how quickly. Less friction (ice) means a smaller net force and a slower velocity change, so Puck A coasts farther — the same logic used earlier when comparing surfaces for friction.

hints.en: Both pucks experience an unbalanced force (friction) opposing their motion. What differs between the two surfaces?
A smaller net force changes velocity more slowly — which surface gives the smaller friction force?
